lead: A program is written twice. The first writing is a plan: a list of plain steps that says what goes in, what is done with it, and what comes out. The second writing is code. The plan is cheap to change; code is not. So the plan carries an algorithm (finite, ordered, unambiguous steps with a clear stop), a flowchart (those steps as a picture), and pseudocode (those steps in plain English). A problem analysis chart sorts the inputs, outputs and processing before either. Every program, from a shop bill to a UPI payment, passes through this stage.

sections.h3: Algorithm: a list of steps that stops

blocks.text: An algorithm is a finite, ordered set of unambiguous steps that has a clear stop. Four words carry the weight. Finite: it ends. Ordered: step 3 runs after step 2. Unambiguous: two people reading it take the same action. Stop: there is a defined end point.
Every algorithm is built from three control constructs:

items: Sequence: do A, then B, then C.
Selection: if a condition holds, take one path, otherwise the other.
Repetition: repeat steps while a condition holds.

blocks.text: A shop bill is pure sequence. A pass/fail mark sheet needs selection. Adding the prices of 100 items needs repetition. Every program you will write is a mix of these three.

sections.h3: Flowchart: the algorithm as a picture

blocks.text: A flowchart draws the steps and joins them with arrows that show the order. Each shape has one fixed job.

head: Symbol
Meaning
rows: Decision, one arrow out per answer

blocks.text: A diamond has two exits, labelled Yes and No. A rectangle has one exit. A flowchart is read from the start oval downwards; every path must reach a stop oval. If two paths exist, both must end.

sections.h3: Pseudocode and the problem analysis chart

blocks.text: Pseudocode writes the steps in plain English with a fixed shape. Keywords go in capitals and indentation shows what is inside a block: IF condition THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF for selection, WHILE condition ... ENDWHILE for repetition. Pseudocode is language-free, so it never contains Python syntax.

blocks.code:
READ pens, notebooks
bill ← pens × 12 + notebooks × 45
PRINT bill

blocks.text: Some syllabi call the written plan a problem analysis chart: four boxes for inputs, required outputs, processing, and alternative solutions. Fill the boxes before you draw anything. The processing box is where the algorithm is born.

figure.caption: The plan for the shop bill. Read it downwards: the arrow into a shape is the order, and the calculation box produces ₹126 for 3 pens and 2 notebooks.

spec.aria: A flowchart that starts, reads the number of pens and notebooks, computes the bill at 12 and 45 rupees each, prints it and stops.
spec.title: Plan for the shop bill

examples.question: A shop sells a pen for ₹12 and a notebook for ₹45. Write pseudocode and draw the plan for a program that reads the number of pens and notebooks bought and prints the bill. Test the plan with 3 pens and 2 notebooks.
steps: Inputs: pens = 3 and notebooks = 2. Unit prices: pen = ₹12, notebook = ₹45.
examples.answer: The bill for 3 pens and 2 notebooks is ₹126.

examples.question: Write the pseudocode that would print Pass if total ≥ 40 and Fail otherwise.
steps: The plan needs selection, because one of two outputs is chosen.
IF total ≥ 40 THEN PRINT Pass ELSE PRINT Fail ENDIF.
In a flowchart this is one diamond with two labelled exits, each leading to its own output parallelogram.
examples.answer: Selection, written with IF ... THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF.

traps: A decision drawn in a rectangle: the branches disappear and the marks go with them.
Writing Python syntax such as print(x) inside pseudocode. Pseudocode is language-free.
Forgetting the stop oval, or leaving one branch of a decision without a stop.
Calling a process an input. Parallelogram for reading or printing, rectangle for calculating.
Writing steps that never end or are vague ("add the prices till done"). That is not an algorithm.

quiz.q: Define an algorithm in one line.
quiz.a: A finite, ordered set of unambiguous steps that has a clear stop.

quiz.q: Which flowchart symbols are used for a decision and for output?
Why can a decision not be drawn inside a rectangle?
quiz.a: A rectangle is a process with a single exit. A decision needs two exits, one per answer, so the flow can branch.

quiz.q: A plan says: keep doubling x until it is large. Give two reasons this is not an algorithm.
quiz.a: "Large" is ambiguous, so two readers act differently, and no stop condition guarantees the steps end.

quiz.q: A pen costs ₹12. Write pseudocode that reads 5 pen counts and prints their total bill.
quiz.a: total ← 0; repeat 5 times: READ n, total ← total + n × 12; PRINT total. For counts 1,2,3,4,5 the total is 15 pens, so ₹180.

quiz.q: A module must print Pass or Fail, then print the mark for every student. Name the constructs used and where each appears.
quiz.a: Repetition over the students (WHILE ... ENDWHILE), and inside it selection (IF ... THEN ... ELSE ... ENDIF). Two input steps read the data, and the printing is a sequence of two outputs after the decision.

beyond: Not for the exam. Flowcharts stop being readable past a page, so industry draws the same idea as a BPMN process diagram or a UML activity diagram, both of which keep the oval, rectangle and diamond but add lanes for who does what. Pseudocode survives as the design note inside a ticket or a pull request. Search next for BPMN, UML activity diagrams and structured programming constructs.
